title: Gentler depth without technique-hopping
point: If going deeper is too much, take a gentler step in the same caring relationship rather than switching to another intense technique to prove you can take it.
where: Safety and Readiness > Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep
quote: Some people try one technique after another instead, to prove to themselves they can take it. Your little one may have had to just take it back then, though. Now there's a grown-up around who can say, "Okay, that's enough for today,"

title: Come outward before re-entering
point: If you can't stop and return, or going in keeps making things worse, come all the way back to the room first and return later when comfortable.
where: Safety and Readiness > Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep
quote: So can you stop in the middle and come back to the room? If you can't, or going in at all keeps making it worse, I'd come all the way back out first.

title: A paused practice has a remembered starting point
point: When you pause child contact, note what prompted it and how far you had got, and restart at that level or gentler.
where: Safety and Readiness > Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep
quote: If you need a break from the communion, simply jot down the reason and the progress made so far. Then come back later, once that reason has changed and you feel comfortable.
missing: The guide has the written reason and progress and a later return once the reason has changed, but never says to resume from that recorded level or gentler (not at full depth).

title: Difficulty and harm differ
point: A hard session is not automatically harmful and a pleasant one is not automatically safe or enough; judge by willingness and aftereffects.
where: Safety and Readiness > Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep > When Therapy Stirs Things Up
quote: It's a bit like going to the gym. You want to make gains, and sore muscles the next day can be good, but proper range of (e)motion here is also key to avoid injury.
missing: Says a stormy session can be fine and that you should check willingness and the next days, but never says a pleasant or calming session is not automatically safe or sufficient.

title: Look at recovery over the next days
point: Judge a session by sleep, ordinary functioning, willingness to return and whether it felt workable, not by how it felt at the time.
where: Safety and Readiness > Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep > When Therapy Stirs Things Up
quote: Keep track of how you feel over the next few days, like how refreshing your sleep is, and how easy it feels to get through your day. Do you want to go back toward what came up, or is some part of you saying no?

title: Adapt before escalating
point: If the effect is unclear, make the next session a little easier and change one thing; if functioning is deteriorating, reduce several demands and get support.
where: Safety and Readiness > Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep > When Therapy Stirs Things Up
quote: If you can't quite tell yet what feels different, I'd just make the next session simpler, one change at a time, like a science nerd, so you learn what made the difference.
missing: The unclear-effect step (simpler session, one change) is there, but not the deteriorating-functioning case: reduce several demands at once and seek appropriate support (the guide only says change course sooner if it is making things worse).

title: Dreams are present experience, not reconstructed facts
point: Dreams and imagery can show current needs and feelings but are not evidence that a depicted past event happened.
where: Safety and Readiness > Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep > When Therapy Stirs Things Up
quote: Sometimes they show what feels missing, or what feels needed. Although sometimes dreams can show you real memories and even predict the future on occasion, we need to be careful not to assume that they are doing that each time.

title: Reach toward real human connection
point: If isolation was part of the hurt, reaching toward people now is itself a way of caring for your little one and need not wait until you are healed.
where: Safety and Readiness > Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep
quote: If being alone was a big part of what hurt during your childhood, I'd call somebody now, mess and all, since reaching toward people is part of taking care of your little one too.

title: More than one safe place to belong
point: Keep good existing relationships while adding other communities, and be wary of any group or person demanding to be your only support.
where: Bringing Reparenting Into Real Life > Finding People and Building Trust > People? Where Are the People?
quote: Keep the good people you've already got. Then maybe try a class, or a spiritual community if you find one that fits you. And if any group, or any one person, starts acting like they should be your only support

title: Short relief must not perpetuate severe pain
point: In an unbearable pain episode, urgent medical assessment and possible pain relief are the caring alternative to a quick fix known to make things worse, even if earlier tests found nothing.
where: When the Practice Gets Difficult > Physical Pain Makes It Harder
quote: the best time to get diagnostics done could be right at the actual time of the crisis, rather than waiting until you feel well enough to make an appointment, and they may be able to treat it while it's happening.
missing: Names the harmful quick fix and says crisis-time diagnostics may bring treatment, but never ties these together as the alternative to repeating the known-worse self-medication, nor says to contact urgent medical services for relief during the episode.

title: Support is not a shortcut to romantic intimacy
point: Friendship and steady support can grow while romance waits; romance comes from mutual love and does not rescue you or reward healing, though you need not be fully healed first.
where: Bringing Reparenting Into Real Life > Finding People and Building Trust > Dating While You Heal
quote: That doesn't mean you have to be completely healed before you date, but romance should follow when two people really love each other and want to build a life together. It won't rescue you from the pain or reward you for healing

title: A chronic pain pathway, not daily emergency calls
point: Frequent severe pain needs an ongoing specialist pathway and a written flare plan with the ER as backup; normal tests do not make the pain imaginary.
where: When the Practice Gets Difficult > Physical Pain Makes It Harder
quote: I'd ask for a chronic pain specialist and a written plan for the flare-ups you can see coming, including the new or severe signs that mean you go to the ER right away

title: Protective medical agency after coercive or harmful care
point: After harmful or coercive care, choose whom to approach and what to share, favoring trusted voluntary support and a chosen advocate over default family or repeat psychiatric routes, while real imminent danger still gets immediate protection.
where: Bringing Reparenting Into Real Life > Speaking Up and Handling Conflict > Being Your Own Advocate With Doctors
quote: If you don't feel up to it, bring someone you trust to speak up for you (like, not that relative who never respected your wishes), and ask what a treatment's for.
missing: Has the chosen advocate and not defaulting to a disrespectful relative, but not that past harmful or coercive treatment changes whom to approach and what to disclose, nor the warning against returning to the same psychiatric pathway or presenting pain-triggered passing thoughts as a plan or bargaining chip.

title: Gratitude is essential ongoing cultivation; the child is not required to perform it
point: Gratitude, from small goods through suffering itself, is an ongoing essential practice felt as heart-softening (not positive reframing), then used to invite the little one in, without forcing it or excusing harm.
where: Building Your Inner Adult > The Nurturer > Ask God for a Loan > Your Loan is PRE-APPROVED!
quote: Genuinely cultivated gratitude (not just empty/forced ritual) is one way to experience divine love for the first time, or to get it back when the feeling fades. I think it's essential if we want to live in that love instead of occasionally visiting it.

title: A drug peak that changes nothing
point: A drug peak reached while holding every attachment and the anger is not the unconditional love the practice aims at; ask whether anything was let go.
where: Altered States and Intensive Practice > What to Do With a Peak
quote: I'd prefer to ask if any of the discontent has been let go, or the anger? If not, that peak was less the love we're after here than "I'll be grateful once I've got it all,"

title: "If only I had X"
point: Gratitude that waits for conditions never arrives; ask what someone would need before they could feel love or gratitude and whether that list ever ends.
where: Building Your Inner Adult > The Nurturer > Ask God for a Loan > Your Loan is PRE-APPROVED! > Mo' Money, Mo' Problems
quote: Because getting what you want is an endless loop, and it doesn't lead to being content with less.
missing: Names conditional gratitude and the endless loop of wanting, but does not offer the question to ask someone who postpones gratitude (what would you need before you could feel it, and does that list ever end).

title: Bringing gratitude in without pushing it
point: Offer gratitude sideways and at times, return to it later if resisted, using small concrete questions, and work toward contradictions from the love side.
where: Building Your Inner Adult > The Nurturer > Ask God for a Loan > Your Loan is PRE-APPROVED!
quote: Being thankful shouldn't be pushed on people who just need to grieve for the moment.
missing: Only the not-pushing and the toxic-positivity disclaimer are there. Missing: coming back to it later when resisted, example small questions (smallest part of a better life, moment-by-moment peace, grateful for a past partner), that ignoring every positive is also toxic, and working a contradiction like 'I love everyone, I hate my dad' from the love side.

title: Gratitude in a calm altered state
point: In a calm, safe, clear altered state gratitude can be practiced as when sober; if overwhelming settle first, and with impaired capacity or a medical concern put safety first.
where: Building Your Inner Adult > The Nurturer > Ask God for a Loan > Your Loan is PRE-APPROVED!
quote: On the other hand, I've noticed that I can sometimes completely flip a bad psychedelic trip into a good one with gratitude alone.
missing: Only a personal anecdote of gratitude turning a bad trip. Missing: that gratitude in a calm altered state is practiced as sober, and the conditions: settle first while overwhelmed, safety and care first with impaired capacity or a medical concern.

title: Hypnosis isn't ruled out by grief or an altered state
point: Hypnosis can suit grieving or altered-state readers depending on type, level of grief and above all purpose (reaching blocked feelings versus escaping), while deep inner-child work waits until grief is less raw.
missing: Nothing on hypnosis during fresh grief or an altered state; the guide only says gentle meditation or self-hypnosis calms the nervous system and is not for all-day coping. Missing: fit depends on kind, grief level and purpose; hypnosis to reach numb feelings can help, to escape is less useful; deep inner-child work waits until grief is less raw.
note_after: Left out as I recommended in turn 119 (the guide never raises whether hypnosis suits someone grieving); his reply of 09:42 answered the other point and raised no objection.

title: Reparenting is not an exercise
point: Reparenting is the ongoing adult-to-child relationship lived in boundaries and everyday choices, not an exercise to finish; meditations are ways of practicing it, not its measure.
where: Understanding Reparenting > Five Stages of Reparenting
quote: Reparenting isn't an exercise you finish, even if you make excellent progress. You might feel like you've mastered the adult/child inner relationship, and then it's Friday night and your boss asks you to stay late again.

title: Keeping yourself safe is part of the work, not a separate track
point: Everyday protective steps (leaving, resting, boundaries, company) are the adult protecting the child and so are reparenting, while outside help stays its own thing.
where: Building Your Inner Adult > Protecting and Building Trust With Your Little One
quote: Even with little or no warmth for your little one yet, the relationship can start with the Protector's plain acts and the warmth can come after

title: Before sharing something legally or personally sensitive
point: Before disclosing highly sensitive material, know that digital records persist, some professionals must report, ask what must be reported and documented first, and still disclose current danger.
where: Bringing Reparenting Into Real Life > Finding People and Building Trust > Opening Up Honestly to the Right People at the Right Pace > Before You Tell the Hardest Stuff
quote: So I'd ask this person, before handing over any tricky specifics: "What does the law require you to report?" That's a normal and expected question.
missing: Missing: asking what gets documented and who can access records; legal privilege versus professional confidentiality; seeking qualified legal advice for legal exposure; AI chats and apps as a retained medium. The guide also says it wouldn't bother asking, and suggests recasting as a dream narrative.

title: Ask what help could actually change, and what a practice actually did
point: After repeated failed care tie a new referral to a specific benefit, learn how a helpful practice worked before warning, keep dreams apart from waking testimony, treat relapse as changed conditions, and don't take coaching support as proof a product works.
where: When the Practice Gets Difficult > How Would You Know It's Helping?
quote: Don't be afraid to ask your therapist/yourself, "What is this practice supposed to help, and how would I know if it's helping?"
missing: Has asking what a practice is for and whether it helps, and caution about dreams and vivid memories elsewhere. Missing: tying a further non-urgent referral to a specific benefit or different expertise, learning how a practice that helped affected the person and its drawbacks, reading a relapse after long improvement as changed conditions rather than shame, and that a coach's personal support is not proof a product works.

title: Make existing partial regulation usable outside the exercise
point: A small release of body tension doesn't prove anxiety is gone; notice the specific effect, whether continuing changes it, how long it lasts and what carries into life, and keep a tiny list of tested supports when overwhelmed.
where: When the Practice Gets Difficult > How Would You Know It's Helping?
quote: And if the therapy is actually working, it should improve your daily life, and especially the health of the inner child-inner adult relationship.
missing: Has carry-over to daily life as the test and that calmer feelings alone are only initial progress. Missing: that a small bodily release doesn't prove the whole anxiety state is gone; noticing specific effect, effect of continuing and how long benefit lasts; keeping a tiny list of already-tested accessible supports when overwhelmed.

title: Protect from relapse by understanding the need, not repeating how to stop
point: Stopping a harmful coping habit differs from not resuming it under distress; ask what it supplies at the critical moment, what non-harmful experiences can meet part of that, and whether a protective step reduces access.
where: Discovering and Healing Old Patterns > How Distrust Reproduces
quote: With any of these patterns, I'd ask what it's protecting you from, because it doesn't really help to just label it a bad habit.
missing: Has asking what a coping pattern is protecting you from. Missing: the distinction between being able to stop and avoiding resuming under distress, finding already-known non-harmful experiences that meet part of the need, and a low-friction step that reduces real-world access (without promises or coercive relocation).

title: Notice feelings, choose actions without self-condemnation
point: A feeling can arise unchosen; examine it kindly and decline to act when it conflicts with consent, safety or a trusted boundary, which is self-protection, not a defect.
where: Practicing With Your Little One > What to Make of a Passing Feeling
quote: "I feel attracted" or "I feel ashamed" is real as a feeling, but it doesn't settle who you are, or who you love.
missing: Has feelings not defining you and unwanted thoughts not making you bad (funeral jingle). Missing: deciding not to act on a feeling when it conflicts with consent, safety, vulnerability or a trusted boundary and calling that mature self-protection, separating feelings, intentions, actions and risks, and not inferring the origin of an attraction from unverified memories or promising a cure.

title: Shame appraisal, realistic repair and selective belonging
point: Separate social rejection from moral rightness, initial shame from self-attack, own precise responsibility and possible repair, and consider leaving groups that repeatedly reject you unjustly.
where: Discovering and Healing Old Patterns > How to Forgive Without Forgetting > Forgiving Yourself
quote: Own what you did (only what was really yours), and let yourself feel the remorse. Repair what you can, by apologizing or making amends, and by changing behavior going forward.
missing: Responsibility, repair, ashamed-of-being-ashamed, shame as a signal versus intrusive-thought shame, pressured forgiveness, belonging bargains and breaks from groups are scattered across sections. Not stated: that actual or feared social rejection is a separate question from whether you were morally wrong, and the instruction not to prescribe disclosure to unpredictable or hostile audiences or to split blame numerically.

title: Choosing whom to tell, and where an AI helper stops
point: Choose a confidant by ease with hard subjects, test with a general version first, ask a therapist what they must report, find an early-sexual-trauma therapist, handle accidental illegal material properly, and know an AI helper has limits.
where: Bringing Reparenting Into Real Life > Finding People and Building Trust > Opening Up Honestly to the Right People at the Right Pace
quote: People can earn more of you by how they handle the smaller stuff, like whether that thing you told them about your weird fear of birds turns into a joke at the next party
missing: Has earned trust through smaller truths and asking what a professional must report. Missing: choosing the listener by ease with difficult subjects rather than closeness, opening with the general kind of thing and asking if they are open to more, seeking a therapist experienced in early sexual trauma without needing certainty, not saving or sharing illegal material seen by accident, and that an AI helper has limits and should say so.

title: Go back over what each person said and did before judging a reaction
point: Before deciding what someone's reaction means, reconstruct in order what each person said and did, including your own words and actions.
where: Bringing Reparenting Into Real Life > Speaking Up and Handling Conflict > Write It. Don't Send It Yet.
quote: Sometimes folks are shocked at the response they get (why does everyone always reject me?), without even considering whether that response was easily predictable based on the energy they gave out to spark it.
missing: Has weighing your own contribution to a reaction and not judging by one fight. Missing: the step of going back over what each person actually said and did, in order, before deciding what the reaction means.

title: How this guide differs from schema therapy
point: The guide keeps three schema-therapy ideas and differs by using the reader's own words rather than schemas, not guessing history from labels, having the reader do the reparenting, not fighting any part, and not claiming schema-therapy research supports it.
where: Conclusion and Appendix > Appendix > Schema Therapy
quote: So the schema therapist takes answers from a questionnaire you fill out and maps your difficulties onto a set list of 18 schemas, which themselves map onto a set of modes, like the Vulnerable Child or the Punitive Parent.
missing: Has the kept ideas, the questionnaire and 18 schemas/modes, history assumed from labels, borrowed adulthood and a note on a more combative stance. Missing: that here you describe parts in your own words and your history is what you tell; that any helper hands reparenting back; that no part is fought or expelled and a harsh critic's contempt need not be obeyed; and the statement that schema-therapy research does not show this guide works.

title: After a painful disagreement, ask what you aimed for, what you expected and how you judge it now
point: Looking back on a hurtful disagreement, set side by side your aim, expected response and present judgment; you can stand by your view, wish you'd said it differently and accept a consequence.
where: Bringing Reparenting Into Real Life > Speaking Up and Handling Conflict > Write It. Don't Send It Yet.
quote: Be honest with yourself about what your goal is for this communication. Do you want to break someone mighty down? To show that you or your views matter? Or do you want them to listen and hear you without getting defensive?
missing: The aim question is asked before sending. Missing: the retrospective look at what you aimed for, what response you expected and how you now judge what you said and what followed, and that standing by a conviction, wishing you had expressed it differently and accepting a foreseen consequence can all be true.

title: A critical voice is not automatically a protector, and you can reject the insult without first settling what it is
point: A harsh inner voice may be a learned script, a protector, a cruel real point or a mix; meet it with compassion and firm limits and refuse the contempt without first deciding which.
where: Building Your Inner Adult > Protecting and Building Trust With Your Little One > Protecting from the Parent You Inherited
quote: critical voice might be that inherited parent script, or any outside influence with no concern for your welfare, it could also be trying to protect you from rejection or failure. It may be pointing to a real problem, but in a cruel way.
missing: Has the several possible readings, curiosity about motives, kernels of truth and refusing insults (Mr. Rogers reframing). Missing: stating that you needn't settle which it is before protecting yourself, that it can be several at once, protective aims beyond rejection or failure (belonging, status, control, safety), and asking whether it would make its point without contempt. His "Protecting from the Parent You Inherited" says the critical voice may be the inherited script, an outside influence or a protector, and the curiosity paragraph refuses "its insults and cruelty" while staying open to its kernels of truth: the point is there in his words.
note_after: Turn 120: status set to "in" to match the table in QUEUE-COVERAGE.md, which turn 119 changed after the JSON was written (the counts there, in 15 and partly 18, are the table's).

title: Proactive protection includes a self-critical strategy that is trying to prevent a feared outcome, not every inner critic
point: A self-critical voice counts as protection only when it is working to prevent a feared outcome; an inner critic is not a guard by default.
where: Building Your Inner Adult > Protecting and Building Trust With Your Little One > Protecting from the Parent You Inherited
quote: it could also be trying to protect you from rejection or failure. It may be pointing to a real problem, but in a cruel way.

title: If anger is hard to put into words, try drawing or scribbling it
point: If anger is hard to word, draw or scribble it without making anything recognizable, then see whether a feeling, need, boundary or action has become clearer.
missing: Not in the guide: no mention of drawing or scribbling anger (the practices section offers writing with the other hand only).
note_after: His own line, 2026-11-04 09:42 UTC: "A protective part might grab the pen first, and then it gets that hand until it's had its say, even if all it can do is scribble angrily." (Journal With Each Hand)

title: A deeper spiritual level can bring release, love and reassurance, but is not a source of facts about ordinary life and does not replace discernment
point: A deeper level of wisdom and compassion can bring love and peace, but isn't treated as a source of specific facts or a replacement for discernment.
where: Conclusion and Appendix > Appendix > Internal Family Systems (IFS)
quote: though it can still give the same love, peace, and clarity to whomever accesses it. Where I part ways with IFS is I don't think the Higher Self has any *specific* wisdom that can be followed mechanically.
